## Extension Hooks

**Optional Hook**: git
Command: `/speckit-git-commit`
Description: Auto-commit after spec clarification

Prompt: Commit clarification changes?
To execute: `/speckit-git-commit`

## Completion Report

**Questions asked & answered**: 4 of a possible 5. You delegated all four to my judgement, so each is recorded in the spec with that delegation noted.

| # | Question | Resolution |
|---|----------|------------|
| 1 | Password hashing function and cost | PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256, 600,000 iterations, 16-byte per-account salt, 32-byte key, constant-time compare |
| 2 | Store file format | UTF-8 JSON object with a format marker, rewritten whole and atomically, owner-only permissions |
| 3 | Error wording for unworded failure paths | One exact string per path, asserted for equality |
| 4 | Per-command latency budget | ≤1 s per command, suite ≤60 s |

**Updated spec**: `specs/001-accounts-cli/spec.md`

**Sections touched**: Clarifications (new), User Scenarios (Stories 1–4 acceptance scenarios), Edge Cases, Functional Requirements (FR-005, FR-006, FR-010, FR-011, FR-018, FR-021, FR-022, FR-025, FR-029; new FR-026a–c and FR-029a–c), Key Entities, Success Criteria (SC-001, SC-002; new SC-009), Assumptions.

The error-string decision had the widest reach: six failure paths said only "reports the problem on standard error", which left nothing for a test to assert against despite Principle III demanding exactly that. Those are now `invalid username`, `password too short`, `username already exists`, `no such account`, `missing password input`, a fixed usage line, and a `store unusable: ` prefix (prefix fixed, cause appended, so the specific problem is still named). I also had to settle a precedence the spec left open — `register` with both a bad username and a short password now prints `invalid username`.

**Spec Quality Checklist**: 16/16 → 16/16 items passing. No markers changed. I did update two of its notes, because they had become false: the old carve-out asserted that "no requirement prescribes internal structure, modules, algorithms or file format", and answers 1 and 2 do precisely that. Rather than quietly leave a wrong justification or fail an item the spec doesn't actually need fixing for, I recorded an explicit extended carve-out naming FR-026a–c, FR-029a–c and SC-009, with the reasoning for holding them as passing.

**Coverage summary**

| Category | Status |
|----------|--------|
| Functional Scope & Behavior | Clear |
| Domain & Data Model | Resolved (store format, record fields) |
| Interaction & UX Flow | Resolved (exact error strings) |
| Performance | Resolved (SC-009) |
| Scalability | Resolved by assumption (≤1,000 accounts, documented, not asked — low impact) |
| Reliability & Availability | Resolved (atomic write, FR-029b) |
| Security & Privacy | Resolved (FR-026a–c, FR-029c) |
| Observability | Deferred — a local CLI with exit codes and stderr needs no logging/metrics; revisit only if operators ask for an audit trail |
| Integration & External Dependencies | Clear (none) |
| Edge Cases & Failure Handling | Clear |
| Constraints & Tradeoffs | Clear |
| Terminology & Consistency | Clear |
| Completion Signals | Clear |
| Misc / Placeholders | Clear |

Two things worth your attention before planning. First, 600,000 iterations means SC-004's 50 registrations plus 50 logins will take roughly 30 seconds of real hashing — that is correct behavior, not a bug, and it is why I set the suite budget at 60 s; if that feels slow in practice, the honest lever is a lower iteration count, not a test-only shortcut, since FR-026b records the parameters per account. Second, FR-026b's stored parameters are a small deliberate deviation from Principle IV's minimalism: without them, a future cost change would silently reject correct passwords, which Principle II forbids outright.

Nothing Outstanding blocks you. **Suggested next command**: `/speckit-plan`.
